newsitem.title: USA: NYS Assembly sees revs up $2 bln, cites Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: NYS Assembly sees revs up $2 bln, cites Wall Street.

text.p: The New York State Assembly, which forecast on Monday that the state will rake in $2 billion more than expected--over three times more than Gov George Pataki predicted--said its forecasts were moderate.

The Assembly's Ways and Means Committee said Pataki's budget underestimated tax collections by $562 million in fiscal 1997, which ends on March 31, and by $1.462 billion in the next fiscal year. It added the Republican governor has a record of overestimating expenditures.

Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, Assembly Speaker, in prepared remarks, said his forecasts were "middle-of-the-road," noting the Assembly last year more accurately predicted how much the state would get than other entities.

The Assemblyman who chairs the committee, Herman Farrell, D-Manhattan, attributed the gap between the Assembly's estimates and the governor's to the timing of how the state gets its money, saying the state division of budget finished its work before a big rise in income during the last quarter was fully counted.

Richard Marino, an analyst with Standard and Poor's Corp, said that over the past couple of years a pattern had developed in which the legislature typically saw revenues rising faster than the governor.
Pataki looks for the state to collect an extra $650 million windfall from late February until the end of the 1998 fiscal year.

"In our conversations with (the Pataki Administration), they have indicated the forecasts are achievable, based on the result so far," said Marino, adding he would reserve judgment until the forecasts were finalized, likely later this month.

While the Assembly also expects New York State to get more revenues than the Senate, which sees the state collecting an extra $922 million, Silver attributed the surge to an expectation that Wall Street's banks and brokerage houses will continue to produce big profits.

Although the financial sector's earnings are closely linked to how strongly the equities and fixed-income markets perform, Silver predicted that activities like mergers and acquisitions and trading, two areas where fees have been growing faster than in commissions for handling retail accounts, would keep these firms' profits up even if the stock market, which is at lofty levels, were to retreat.
"Thus, even a downturn in the stock market would not have a drastic impact on 1997-98 fiscal year receipts," he said.

Some of this optimism might be questioned, however, by financial analysts. For example, Rosemary Scanlon, the state deputy comptroller for the city, has noted that Wall Street lost jobs in 1994, when the bond market eroded.

And Silver, who noted that the rest of the state continues to lag Wall Street's stellar performance, predicted the state's jobs will only grow by 0.8 percent in 1997, though the nation should see a rise of 1.8 percent.

The Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, who said the big increases in revenues proved the state's big tax reductions were successful, and Silver are expected to soon thrash out a consensus estimate.
